P(Z\le z)=Φ(z).

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-2.20<Z<2.10) & =P(Z<2.10)-P(Z\le -2.20) \\  & =P(Z\le 2.10)-P(Z\le -2.20) \\  & =Φ(2.10)-Φ(-2.20)\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-2.20) & =0.0139, \\ Φ(-2.10) & =0.0179,\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(2.10) & =P(Z\le 2.10) \\  & =1-P(Z\le -2.10) \\  & =1-Φ(-2.10) \\  & =1-0.0179 \\  & =0.9821\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-2.20<Z<2.10) & =Φ(2.10)-Φ(-2.20) \\  & =0.9821-0.0139 \\  & =0.9682.\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14259374/assets/f88bf9a66694858e9eaf16f616555eda6d9da7de9f62b678bc1f03b32bf9a620.png)

For a random variable $Z \sim N(0,1)$ we have the following symmetry property for $a > 0{:}$

$$
P(Z \gt -a) = P(Z \lt a) = \Phi(a)
$$

We're given that $Z\sim N(0,1),$ and we wish to compute $P( Z > -0.76).$ The required probability is represented by the area shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14259374/assets/fbacbbe3f53c73316fd070d95e4c077cd695bdcf884d30a95f6b0850df328c80.png)

By symmetry, this equals the area corresponding to the probability $P(Z \lt 0.76).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14259374/assets/c0f612336c02eee97d6c66b56f0854286b3a23b90053810e9e4fb75b698b5a60.png)

Therefore,

$$
P(Z > -0.76)
= P(Z < 0.76)
= \Phi(0.76)
= 0.7764.
$$

For a random variable $Z \sim N(0,1),$ we have the following symmetry property for $a > 0{:}$

$$
P(Z \gt a) = P(Z \lt -a) = \Phi(-a)
$$

We're given that $Z\sim N(0,1),$ and we wish to compute $P( Z \lt -1.54).$ The required probability is represented by the area shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14259374/assets/52d4c1add91819ff1f9dddf609b5753506c26e6cd6ee7f3cb14150ccb9b60971.png)

By symmetry, this equals the area corresponding to the probability $P(Z \gt 1.54).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14259374/assets/7fef056bb5564986a009198685a2951de87ccb8e09c932c6902bfafdcdf0656f.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z<-1.54) & =P(Z>1.54) \\  & =1-P(Z<1.54) \\  & =1-Φ(1.54) \\  & =1-0.9382 \\  & =0.0618.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We're given that $Z\sim N(0,1),$ and we wish to compute $P(-0.53 <        Z <        0.53).$ The required probability is represented by the area shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14259374/assets/bb86bde3595d6a64d1cd82da3c928f28c496f495f9c6815e56ee025a4a69d685.png)

By the definition of the cumulative distribution function $\Phi(z),$ 

$$
P(Z \leq z) = \Phi(z).
$$

So, we express the required probability in terms of $\Phi(z)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-0.53<Z<0.53) & =P(Z<0.53)-P(Z\le -0.53) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.53)-P(Z\le -0.53) \\  & =Φ(0.53)-Φ(-0.53)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we know that

$$
\Phi(0.53) = 0.7019,
$$

but we are not given $\Phi(-0.53) .$ However, we can compute this using symmetry:

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.53) & =P(Z\le -0.53) \\  & =P(Z\ge 0.53) \\  & =1-P(Z<0.53) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 0.53) \\  & =1-Φ(0.53) \\  & =1-0.7019 \\  & =0.2981\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-0.53<Z<0.53) & =Φ(0.53)-Φ(-0.53) \\  & =0.7019-0.2981 \\  & =0.4038.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose that the continuous random variable $Z$ follows a standard normal distribution:

$$
Z\sim N(0,1)
$$

The standard normal distribution is *symmetric* about the vertical axis. We can use this fact to help us calculate probabilities. 

For example, the two shaded areas below are equal. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14259374/assets/a35ea4ef8148eb515aab632525262293450d04f2f951eeae77d280d423cc5408.png)

Note that

- the shaded area on the left corresponds to $P(Z \lt -a),$ and

- the shaded area on the right corresponds to $P(Z \gt a).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14259374/assets/a0d0524f4578a55f0e3f8db77a1e7dbef48e17693fa1eb03abef65d858b69ed2.png)

Since these two areas are equal by symmetry, we have the following rule:

$$
P(Z \gt a) = P(Z \lt -a)
$$

Similarly, we have that

$$
P(Z \gt -a) = P(Z \lt a) = \Phi(a),
$$

as shown below. Recall that $\Phi(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14259374/assets/3747c80cc9ff23576114e733f80e8d6c275d7387dedc53a895c53307e7aa0eeb.png)

Let's take a look at some concrete examples.
